awd_titl_txt: CAREER: Proteins under Confinement: Revealing the Impact of Spatial Restrictions on Enzyme Structure, Dynamics and Function
awd_abstract_narration:
Proteins are essential macromolecules for many cellular and life processes. In cells, proteins experience a highly crowded and confined environment. Understanding protein structure, dynamics, and function under crowding and confinement is, therefore, critical for understanding the function of these essential macromolecules in nature. This project will a recently developed platform that creates confined space at sizes similar to typical proteins, and use modern spectroscopic methods to examine protein structure and dynamics.  These studies will be used to generate a systematic understanding on how spatial confinement impacts the protein structure-function relationship. This project will improve the communication and collaboration of next generation scientists in North Dakota by through a summer student research exchange program between North Dakota State University and the United Tribes Technical College.  Local undergraduate and high school researchers will also be recruited to participate in the project. Lastly, the project will stimulate the interest in science for local elementary school students.

This project will determine the influence of the size, shape, and boundary properties of spatial confinement on protein structure, dynamics, and function. This project will employ the recently developed MOFs/COFs to create systematically confined spaces that differ in size, shape, and boundary properties, respectively. The loading conditions of two model proteins, lysozyme and the human Cu/Zn superoxide dismutase (SOD1), will be optimized separately in order to optimize their loading capacity. The activities of lysozyme and SOD1 will be determined using standard assays with minor modifications. Site-directed spin labeling will then be utilized to implant spin probes into each model protein. EPR dynamics and long-range distance distribution measurements will then be carried out to determine global and local (the active site and/or substrate pathway) conformational flexibility changes of the two model proteins confined in different MOFs/COFs. SDSL-EPR is ideal for these experiments because it can overcome the complexities caused by MOF/COF backgrounds and protein-MOF/COF interactions and reveal the needed structural information. Correlating the function with the structural details under varied confined conditions will establish the correlation between confinement factors and protein structure-function relationship. 

This project is jointly funded by the Molecular Biophysics cluster of the Division of Molecular and Cellular Biosciences (MCB) and the Established Program to Stimulate Competitive Research (EPSCoR).

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Proteins are essential biological macromolecules whose structures and motions are closely linked to their functions. Thus far, most of current knowledge about proteins comes from studies in dilute solutions, where they are stable and easier to analyze. In living systems, however, proteins rarely operate under such conditions. Instead, they function within spatially confined environments such as cellular compartments, molecular tunnels, and macromolecular condensates, where the available space is comparable to the size of proteins. These confined environments impose geometric restrictions that can significantly influence protein behavior. Directly studying proteins under these conditions inside cells remains challenging due to the complexity of the cellular environment. An alternative is to create well-defined synthetic porous materials that mimic key aspects of biological confinement. Such systems reduce complexity while allowing precise control over factors such as size, shape, and chemical properties, making it possible not only to observe how proteins behave under confinement but also to uncover general physical principles governing how restriction factors influence protein structure and dynamics. Despite this opportunity, a major challenge in molecular biophysics has been the limited ability to directly measure protein structure and dynamics under well-controlled, ideally uniform confinement conditions.

This project addressed this challenge by establishing an experimental framework that enables site-specific measurement of proteins inside confined environments at the nanometer scale. A key innovation is to employ synthetic porous materials, metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) and covalent organic frameworks (COFs). These MOF/COF materials provide precisely defined nanoscale chambers whose size, shape, and chemical properties can be systematically tuned, allowing confinement effects to be examined in a controlled and reproducible manner one confinement factor at a time. Another innovation of this project is the use of site-directed spin labeling (SDSL) in combination with electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy to probe protein behavior at the bio-material interfaces. This approach enables residue-level measurements of protein dynamics, conformational distributions, and intramolecular distances, even when proteins are embedded in heterogeneous solid complex environments. Because proteins in MOF/COF systems prevent the access of many conventional structural biology techniques, SDSL-EPR becomes the optimal approach to access protein structural and dynamic information that is otherwise difficult to obtain. While the approach requires specialized expertise in spectroscopy, protein labeling, and materials design, once established it can be applied broadly to general enzymes to probe their behavior under confinement.

Using this framework, this project showed experimentally that nanoscale confinement can strongly affect enzyme flexibility, structural stability, and catalytic behaviors. Experiments based on model enzymes showed that the chemical properties of the surrounding pore environment significantly affect how the proteins move and perform their function. The project also revealed how different confinement factors, such as volume/dimension, hydrophobicity, and shape, created by MOF/COF systems with varied properties can impact the interplay of the structure, dynamics, and function of model enzymes. These findings provide new insights into how spatial restrictions regulate protein function, which is often encountered in nature, and offer a pathway for quantitatively studying these effects in a controlled, simplified environment outside of cells.

Beyond advancing fundamental understanding, this project also informs the development of enzyme-material hybrid systems, where proteins are immobilized within porous solids for applications in catalysis, biotechnology, and environmental processes. By linking confinement conditions to measurable changes in protein behavior, the project provides guidance for designing materials that better preserve enzyme activity in practical uses.

The project also contributed to workforce development and education across varied levels. A total of nine high school students, thirteen undergraduate students and eight graduate students participated in the research. These trainees gained experience in interdisciplinary approaches crossing biophysics, materials science, and chemical engineering, including experimental design, quantitative analysis, and scientific presentation/communication. The project also contributed to broadening participation in Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) by involving women and first-generation college students in research.

Outreach efforts extended these impacts to a broader community. Activities included mentoring high school students through research programs, delivering lectures at tribal colleges through the NSF-supported Nurturing American Tribal Undergraduate Research and Education (NATURE) Sunday Academy, and participation in programs such as Parents Involvement with Children Nurturing Intellectual Curiosity in Science (PICNICS) and the North Dakota Governor’s School, where students engage in intensive summer research experiences. Additional demonstrations introduced foundational scientific concepts, such as magnetic forces, to younger students, Building early interest in science.

Finally, the project contributed to the broader scientific community by promoting education in advanced spectroscopic techniques. The project resulted in lectures and workshops at universities and institutions and developed educational materials to support the adoption of EPR-based approaches for studying proteins in complex environments.

Overall, this project established a specialized but broadly applicable experimental platform for studying proteins under spatial confinement, enabling measurements that are otherwise difficult to access, advancing understanding of protein behavior in complex environments, and training a diverse group of students in interdisciplinary scientific research.
